study.title: Habakkuk 3 - prayer of fear, memory and trust
study.overview: Habakkuk 3 concludes prophecy as a prayer in the form of song. The prophet responds to the threat of judgment with reverence, recalling God's past interventions in behalf of his people and asking the Lord to renew his work at the right time. The chapter advances from worship to historical remembrance, from the description of the warrior God to the confession of the prophet's weakness, and ends with a firm trust: even though the resources of the earth lack, the Lord remains the strength of salvation.

outline.title: Prayer that calls for renewal and mercy
outline.explanation: The chapter opens as a liturgical prayer. Habakkuk fears the work of God because he recognizes his holiness and sovereignty, but asks that the Lord make known again and, in the midst of wrath, remember mercy.

outline.title: God appears as the divine warrior
outline.explanation: The prophet describes the manifestation of God with images of glory, brightness, plague, pestilence and trembling of the nations. Language recalls God's saving action in the past and shows that creation and peoples do not resist their presence.

outline.title: The Lord Acts to Save His People
outline.explanation: The sequence of poetic questions emphasizes that God is not in conflict with nature, but is marching against the oppressors. He saves his people, smites the leader of the wicked, and, before this revelation, Habakkuk trembles, awaiting the day of anguish with astonishment and submission.

outline.title: Faith that remains without provision
outline.explanation: Even without visible harvests, flocks or livelihood, the prophet decides to rejoice in the Lord. The outcome states that God is his strength and that he will enable him to walk firmly, like a choir in the high places.

study.context: The notes present the chapter as a prayer in the form of a psalm, linked to the crisis announced in previous chapters and focused on the hope of deliverance. The prophet recalls the ancient divine intervention in favor of the people, especially in language that evokes the exodus and the march of God as a warrior in behalf of his own. The closure, directed to the musical conductor, suggests community and liturgical use.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the holiness of God does not eliminate mercy, but sustains it; therefore, the believer can fear divine action and at the same time supplicate renewal. God is presented as sovereign over history, about nations, and on creation, using even judgments as instruments of his redeeming purpose. True faith does not depend on material stability, but on the identity of God as Savior and strength of his people. The mature response to suffering is to remember God's past action, wait for his intervention and rejoice in him even before seeing the visible provision.

scholarViews.insight: Habakkuk 3 ends as a prayer in the style of psalm, and in the final verse the prophet recognizes that all his strength comes from the sovereign Lord, his Savior.
In verse 2, the prophet asks God to renew his known work in the past, remembering mercy in the midst of anger before what will come upon Judah.
In verse 13, God's departure is understood as direct intervention for the salvation of his people; without this divine interference, deliverance would not have happened.

questions: What changes in our prayer when we remember God's works in the past rather than focus only on the present crisis?
How is it possible to rejoice in the Lord when basic resources are lacking, as described in verse 17?
In what situations do we need to ask not only for relief, but also for God to renew his work in the middle of the years?
study.practice: Set aside a time to recount, in writing, three acts of God's faithfulness in your life or in biblical history, and turn it into prayer. Then pray verse 2 asking the Lord to renew his work in his house, church and city, without hiding his reverence and fear. Finally, choose a loss or concrete insecurity that you face today and declare, honestly, that your main joy will continue to be the Lord, not the circumstances.
study.uncertainty: There are interpretative points that the notes deal in different ways: the exact meaning of "Siguionote" is not clarified safely; the references to the Teman, Cusã and Midian are explained in a poetic and historical way, but not in an absolutely unanimous way; and in verse 13 there is a divergence about whether "your anointed" points specifically to Joshua or the people of Israel together. The biblical text presented also brings some poetic formulations whose detailed historical identification cannot be affirmed only based on the notes provided.
